After lunch we got chatting.
I'm getting to like him better now.

glosses: To take or catch (a scheduled transportation service).

examples.text: I normally get the 7:45 train.
I'll get the 9 a.m. [flight] to Boston.

glosses: To respond to (a telephone call, a doorbell, etc).

examples.text: Can you get that call, please? I'm busy.

glosses: (with full infinitive) To be able, be permitted, or have the opportunity (to do something desirable or ironically implied to be desirable).

examples.text: I'm so jealous that you got to see them perform live!
The finders get to keep 80 percent of the treasure.
Great. I get to clean the toilets today.

glosses: To understand. (compare get it)

examples.text: Yeah, I get it, it's just not funny.
I don't get what you mean by "fun". This place sucks!
I mentioned that I was feeling sad, so she mailed me a box of chocolates. She gets me.

glosses: To be told; be the recipient of (a question, comparison, opinion, etc.).

examples.text: "You look just like Helen Mirren." / "I get that a lot."

Do you mind? Excuse me / I saw you over there / Can I just tell you ¶ Although there are millions of / Cephalophores that wander through this world / You've got something extra going on / I think you probably know ¶ You probably get that a lot / I'll bet that people say that a lot to you, girl.

glosses: Used with the past participle to form the dynamic passive voice of a dynamic verb. Compared with static passive with to be, this emphasizes the commencement of an action or entry into a state.

examples.text: He got bitten by a dog.
Of particular importance is the bureaucratic organization of European judiciaries. The judiciary is a career. You start at the bottom and get assigned and promoted at the pleasure of your superiors.

glosses: Used with a pronoun subject, usually you but sometimes one, to indicate that the object of the verb exists, can occur or is otherwise typical.

examples.text: You get some very rude people here.
It was the kind of shop you used to get in most small towns.
He thinks that proper to northern man is the cellular composition, you know, the kind of thing one gets in Celtic ornamentation, for example, which a subject that interests him greatly.
You get non-binary people – you get people who don't identify as a man or a woman.
It was a terrible place to live. You get places like that. It is just the way it is.

glosses: To become ill with or catch (a disease).

examples.text: I went on holiday and got malaria.

glosses: To catch out, trick successfully.

examples.text: He keeps calling pretending to be my boss—it gets me every time.

glosses: To perplex, stump.

examples.text: That question's really got me.

glosses: To find as an answer.

examples.text: What did you get for question four?

glosses: To bring to reckoning; to catch (usually as a criminal); to effect retribution.

examples.text: The cops finally got me.
I'm gonna get him for that.

glosses: To hear completely; catch.

examples.text: Sorry, I didn't get that. Could you repeat it?

glosses: To getter.

examples.text: I put the getter into the container to get the gases.

glosses: To beget (of a father).

examples.text: I had rather to adopt a child than get it.
Thou poisonous slave, got by the devil himself / Upon thy wicked dam, come forth!
Walter had said, dear God, Thomas, it was St fucking Felicity if I'm not mistaken, and her face was to the wall for sure the night I got you.

glosses: To learn; to commit to memory; to memorize; sometimes with out.

examples.text: to get a lesson;  to get out one's Greek lesson
it being harder with him to get one sermon by heart, than to pen twenty

glosses: Used with a personal pronoun to indicate that someone is being pretentious or grandiose.

examples.text: Get her with her new hairdo.
Brother, get her! Draped on a bedspread made from three kinds of fur!
Money's pouring in somewhere, because Churchgate's got lovely new stone setts, and a cultural quarter (ooh, get her) is promised.

glosses: To go, to leave; to scram.

examples.text: Get, now — get! — before I call an officer and lay a charge against ye.

examples.text: They’re coming to get you, Barbara.

And he slashed up Dasher just like Freddy Krueger

glosses: To make acquisitions; to gain; to profit.

examples.text: We mourn, France smiles; we lose, they daily get.

glosses: To measure.

examples.text: Did you get her temperature?

glosses: To cause someone to laugh.

examples.text: It gets me every time!

glosses: Offspring, especially illegitimate.

examples.text: At the time when I am making these observations, one of his colts is the first favourite for the Derby; and it will be recollected, that a filly of his get won the Oaks in 1808.

glosses: Lineage.

Something gotten, something gained or won; an acquisition.

examples.text: I had reconnected with the lust of my life while landing a big get for the magazine.

examples.text: Kylie: Oi, Bono! You lazy get! Have you finished my song yet?

examples.text: In Israel, rabbinic courts can imprison men until they acquiesce and grant gets to their wives.

glosses: comparative form of bad: more bad

examples.text: Your exam results are worse than before.

glosses: comparative form of badly (adverb): more badly

examples.text: The harder you try, the worse you do.

Irregular bedtimes may disrupt healthy brain development in young children, according to a study of intelligence and sleeping habits. ¶ Going to bed at a different time each night affected girls more than boys, but both fared worse on mental tasks than children who had a set bedtime, researchers found.

glosses: Less skillfully.

examples.text: He drives worse than anyone else I know.

glosses: More severely or seriously.

examples.text: The bad news affected me worse than it did my brother.

glosses: Used to start a sentence describing something that is worse.

examples.text: Her leg is infected. Still worse, she's developing a fever.

glosses: Loss; disadvantage; defeat

examples.text: Judah was put to the worse before Israel.

glosses: That which is worse; something less good.

examples.text: Do not think the worse of him for his enterprise.

glosses: To make worse; to put at disadvantage; to discomfit.

examples.text: Weapons more violent, when next we meet, / May serve to better us and worse our foes.
